desc:
You are given an absolute Unix-style file path path that starts with '/'. Return its canonical form.

Split the path at '/' into components. A component is:

  • empty (from repeated slashes such as // or a trailing slash): ignore it,
  • '.': the current directory, so ignore it,
  • '..': go up one directory. At the root, '..' does nothing,
  • anything else, including names such as '...' or 'a.b': a normal directory name.

The canonical path starts with a single '/', joins the remaining directory names with single slashes, and has no trailing slash (except when the answer is the root, which is just '/').

Example: '/a/./b/../../c/' goes into a, stays, goes into b, up to a, up to the root, then into c, so the answer is '/c'.
constraints: path consists of letters, digits, '.', '_' and '/'
No component other than '.' and '..' is ever treated specially (for example '...' is a normal name)
hints: Think of the current location as a list of directory names from the root. What does each kind of component do to that list?
A normal name is appended, '..' removes the last name if there is one, and '' and '.' change nothing.
Split on '/', process the components with a stack, and join the stack with '/' after a leading slash. An empty stack gives '/'.
editorial: The current directory is a path of names, and every operation touches only its end, so a stack is the natural model. Split the string at '/' and handle each component: skip '' and '.', pop for '..' when the stack is not empty (going up from the root stays at the root), and push anything else.

Finally build the answer as '/' + '/'.join(stack). For an empty stack this is just '/', which is correct. Be careful that '...' is a legal name and must be pushed. The work is linear in the length of the path: O(n) time and O(n) space.
